The essence of this theory is that the obstacles to development are formidable and widespread. The development process by its very nature is not a smooth and uninterrupted process. It involves a series of unbalanced 'jumps'. The factors affecting economic growth, although functionally related to each other, are marked by numerous "discontinuities" and "humps." The basic argument of the "big push" theory is that such mutually beneficial expansion of output This is unlikely to happen unless the initial hurdles are overcome. There are various types of "non-appropriabilities" or "insuperabilities" which if not removed through "major efforts" will not allow the emergence and transmission of 'external economies' – which lie behind the self- generated development process. . Professor Rodan distinguishes three types of inseparability and externalities with a view to specifying the areas where large-scale efforts are required. they are: (i) Insuperabilities in the production function, that is, looseness of capital, especially in the formation of social overhead capital. (ii) Indivisibility of demand, i.e., complementarily of demand. (iii) Indivisibility of savings, i.e., disturbance in the supply of savings.
